source: Dungeons & Dividends rulebook, Draft v1, as supplied by the repo owner. Sections cited per entry. This file is a transcription of that document, not an interpretation of it.
confidenceNote: A house game system, not a financial standard. Nothing here is advice; the mechanics are a lens on numbers computed elsewhere in the suite.
note: Rulebook content, PLUS a bestiary extension written for this build. Every creature added here carries "origin": "extension" — anything without that field came from the rulebook as supplied. Every dollar-to-score threshold lives in dnd_scoring.json, not here.

triageTechniques.name: Avalanche Triage
triageTechniques.detail: Target the highest-APR balance first. The best save bonus against the single largest balance; mathematically optimal, slowest visible first win.

triageTechniques.name: Snowball Triage
triageTechniques.detail: Target the smallest balance first. A smaller save bonus, but success grants temporary Inspiration — behavioral momentum modeled as a real mechanic.

triageTechniques.name: Consolidation Triage
triageTechniques.detail: Merge balances into one instrument. A one-time reduction of a full Debt Burden Level on success, but future incremental saves against the consolidated balances stop.

revenueGuild.blurb: The tax system is a Faction, not a Monster: a lawful, rules-based organization with its own ranks and its own win condition (compliance), not a hunger for your money specifically.

revenueGuild.neutralGround: Appeals and Tax Court aren't encounters — they're an arena you can invoke instead of accepting the Department's ruling. It costs resources (usually a companion) but resets the outcome to a fresh judgment.
revenueGuild.standing: Faction Standing is a separate meter from your six stats. Round-number deductions, home-office claims, a cash-heavy business, and aggressive Schedule C losses lower it. Clean multi-year history, consistent numbers, and e-filing raise it.

statusEffects.name: Means-Tested Benefit
statusEffects.restricts: The Benefits Cliff — cross the line and the entire benefit can vanish at once
statusEffects.duration: Ends when income/assets cross the threshold

benefitsCliff: Several statuses don't taper. Cross the income or asset line by even a small amount and the whole benefit can vanish — a small raise costing far more in lost benefits than it provides. It plays like a trap dealing damage proportional to the benefit lost, not the size of the trigger, and it is exactly what Scenario Foresight exists to see coming.

outcomes: 3 successes → Stabilized. HP resets to 1. You found a way out — sold something, borrowed, cut spending hard.
3 failures → Insolvency. Forced bankruptcy or default. Not game over, but it costs Level and leaves a lasting debuff.
Natural 20 equivalent (an unexpected windfall while at 0) → instantly stabilize and regain 1 HP.
Natural 1 equivalent (a second crisis while already down) → counts as two failures.
A Companion (bankruptcy attorney, debt counselor, a family member able to lend) can auto-stabilize you once.
deathSaves.massiveDamage: If a single hit deals damage equal to or greater than your Max HP in one shot, you skip death saves entirely and go straight to Insolvency. This is why AC (insurance) matters more than raw HP against the biggest monsters.
recovery: Short Rest (a pay cycle) — regain HP equal to (income − expenses) for that cycle, if positive.
Long Rest (a strong, uninterrupted month or quarter) — regain HP up to max, contingent on a CON save.
Potion (a windfall) — heals a fixed amount immediately, no rest required.
deathSaves.temporaryHp: A windfall sitting in checking that hasn't been moved into real reserves. Absorbs the next hit first, doesn't stack with itself, and evaporates at your next Long Rest if not converted into permanent HP.

encounterRules.note: BRIEF §9.3. The rulebook's own §13 leaves save DCs unset, so they are derived from CR here rather than invented per monster — one ladder, visible, arguable. Damage is expressed in HP, and HP is weeks (D-046), so every damage figure is already in weeks of runway.
encounterRules.source: The ladder follows the shape of a CR-to-save-DC progression: harder monster, harder save. The numbers are a convention chosen here, not a measurement and not agreed elsewhere — argue with them by editing this array.

d20.note: A natural 1 always fails and a natural 20 always succeeds, so the chance a hit lands is clamped to 5%-95% however lopsided the numbers get.

tiers.name: Getting off the floor
tiers.about: Stop the bleeding and build the first buffer. Nothing else on this list works while a balance is compounding faster than you can pay it.
tiers.looksLike: Every shock is a crisis, because there is nothing between you and it.
tiers.endsWhen: A month of expenses exists somewhere you can reach it, and no debt is growing faster than you can pay it down.
tiers.biggestRisk: Small, constant, unnoticed damage — the creatures here do 1d4 and never announce themselves.

tiers.name: Building the engine
tiers.about: Widen the gap between what arrives and what leaves, then make the gap move on its own.
tiers.looksLike: You can absorb one bad month. Two would hurt. The saving still depends on you remembering.
tiers.endsWhen: The saving happens without you, the employer match is captured, and a full emergency fund is in place.
tiers.biggestRisk: Your own raises. This is where lifestyle creep does its best work, because every head it grows is reasonable.

tiers.name: Protecting the pile
tiers.about: Stop losing it. The pile is now big enough that protecting it beats adding to it.
tiers.looksLike: A good year adds more than you earn. A bad one could take back several.
tiers.endsWhen: A bad year is survivable without selling anything, and no single event — health, job, one holding — can take a third of it.
tiers.biggestRisk: Concentration and the things insurance exists for. The creatures here hit for 4d8 and up.

tiers.name: Living off it
tiers.about: Turn a pile into an income, and work out what it was for.
tiers.looksLike: The maths works. The question stops being how much and starts being when, and then why.
tiers.endsWhen: It doesn't. This is the part you were saving for.
tiers.biggestRisk: Order, not average. The same returns in the wrong sequence are a different retirement.

effects.negate: The attack cannot land at all.
effects.advantage: You roll the save twice and keep the better — worth about +3.7 on average, applied here as a flat bonus.

exhaustion.note: BRIEF §9.7. The rulebook names "Exhausted" once — as what the Unemployed status decays into — and never defines it. This ladder is written for this build to fill that gap, and is marked origin: extension. It is DERIVED from runway, never self-declared: exhaustion is not a mood, it is what a thin buffer costs you in decisions you can no longer afford to make well.
exhaustion.savePenaltyNote: Each level subtracts from every saving throw. Being close to the edge really does make you easier to move: you cannot wait for a better offer, shop the policy, or walk away, and every creature in the bestiary is built to exploit exactly that.

levels.label: Rested
levels.effect: You can afford to say no, wait, and shop around. That is what the buffer buys.
levels.tell: A bad week is an annoyance.

levels.label: Watchful
levels.effect: You check the balance before ordinary purchases. Small friction, but the deciding has started to cost something.
levels.tell: You know roughly what is in the account without looking.

levels.label: Stretched
levels.effect: Timing starts to drive choices instead of price. You take the option that is available now over the one that is better.
levels.tell: You have begun paying more to pay later.

levels.label: Cornered
levels.effect: You can no longer walk away from a bad deal, which is the condition every predator in the bestiary is built for.
levels.tell: A single unexpected bill would change the month.

levels.label: Running on fumes
levels.effect: Decisions are made in order of what is due next. Interest rates stop being a factor you can weigh.
levels.tell: You are choosing which bill is late.

levels.label: Spent
levels.effect: Every option costs more than it should, because every option is now urgent. This is where the most expensive money in the world gets borrowed.
levels.tell: Less than a week of cover left.

levels.label: Down
levels.effect: At 0 HP. Death saves, not decisions — see the Death Saves rules.

statusNote: BRIEF §9.7. Status effects are SELF-DECLARED, like alignment — they are facts about your situation that no number in the household can see. Nothing here is computed and nothing is inferred; if you have not said, the sheet says you have not said.
